title: Blood Product Identification: Match Patient, Product, and Order
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Wrong-patient or wrong-component transfusion can be catastrophic. Follow the facility's positive patient-identification and blood-component verification process exactly before starting any transfusion.
recognize: Mismatched identifiers, unclear compatibility status, an unreadable label, or an order/product discrepancy are stop points.
priorities: Verify the order, patient identity, blood product, compatibility requirements, expiration, and required independent check before initiation.
assessMonitor: Confirm baseline vital signs and relevant history per policy before starting.
interventions: Do not begin until every identification discrepancy is resolved.
medicationSafety: Never bypass the second-person/electronic verification process required by policy.
teaching: Explain that repeated identity checks are intentional safety steps.
delegationScope: Blood-administration authority varies by state/facility; identification and monitoring must follow authorized role and competency.
examTrap: Starting because the unit looks correct and the patient verbally confirms their name.
sourceBasis: FDA blood and blood-component safety framework

title: Early Transfusion Monitoring: Stay Close for the First Change
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Many serious transfusion reactions begin with nonspecific symptoms. Follow facility policy for early observation and vital-sign monitoring, and treat new fever, chills, dyspnea, back/chest pain, hypotension, rash, anxiety, or rigors as possible reaction cues.
recognize: New symptoms temporally associated with transfusion require prompt assessment rather than reassurance.
priorities: Remain available for early assessment and know the immediate stop/escalation workflow.
assessMonitor: Trend vital signs, respiratory status, skin findings, pain, urine changes, and overall patient response.
interventions: Escalate any suspected reaction immediately and follow the transfusion-reaction protocol.
medicationSafety: Premedication history never rules out a transfusion reaction.
teaching: Tell patients to report any new sensation or symptom immediately during transfusion.
delegationScope: Monitoring responsibilities depend on facility policy and authorized blood-administration role.
examTrap: Assuming mild chills are expected and continuing without reassessment.
oneLinePearl: New symptoms during transfusion are a reaction until evaluated.

title: Suspected Transfusion Reaction: Stop and Escalate
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: When a transfusion reaction is suspected, stop the blood product and initiate the facility reaction protocol immediately while maintaining patient support and notifying the appropriate clinical/blood-bank team.
recognize: Fever, chills, rash, dyspnea, chest/back pain, hypotension, wheeze, anxiety, rigors, hemoglobinuria, or sudden overload symptoms can signal a reaction.
priorities: Stop the transfusion, support ABCs, notify the RN/provider and transfusion service, and preserve tubing/product specimens as policy directs.
assessMonitor: Repeat vital signs, respiratory status, urine output/color, skin findings, pain, and response to intervention.
interventions: Follow the ordered reaction workup and emergency treatment pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not restart the same unit unless the formal protocol and responsible clinician explicitly authorize it.
teaching: Explain that stopping the transfusion is a precaution while the cause is evaluated.
delegationScope: Reaction recognition/escalation is licensed-nurse work; blood-product handling follows transfusion-service policy.
examTrap: Slowing the infusion instead of stopping it when a reaction is suspected.
oneLinePearl: Suspect reaction: stop first, then sort out which reaction.

title: Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction: Think Incompatibility
bottomLine: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions can progress rapidly to shock, DIC, and kidney injury. Stop the transfusion and escalate immediately when fever/chills, severe back or flank pain, chest discomfort, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, or unexplained bleeding develops.
recognize: Symptoms may begin soon after incompatible red-cell exposure and can be severe even with a small volume.
priorities: Stop the transfusion, support circulation, notify the transfusion service/provider, and follow the hemolysis workup protocol.
assessMonitor: Monitor hemodynamics, urine output/color, bleeding, renal function/labs as ordered, and mental status.
interventions: Maintain supportive care and prepare for protocol-driven laboratory evaluation and treatment.
medicationSafety: Never treat symptoms while allowing the suspect unit to continue.
teaching: Future transfusions require careful review of transfusion history and compatibility testing.
delegationScope: Immediate reaction response requires licensed clinical judgment and transfusion-team collaboration.
examTrap: Attributing dark urine and back pain to dehydration while the transfusion continues.
oneLinePearl: Pain + hypotension + dark urine during transfusion = stop now.

title: TACO: Volume Overload After Transfusion
bottomLine: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload presents with acute respiratory distress and volume-overload findings related to transfusion. Older adults and patients with cardiac/renal impairment may be especially vulnerable; stop/escalate when overload is suspected.
recognize: Dyspnea, hypoxemia, hypertension or other hemodynamic change, crackles, edema, and worsening pulmonary congestion after transfusion raise concern.
priorities: Stop or pause per reaction protocol, position/support breathing, notify the responsible team, and follow the TACO evaluation/treatment pathway.
assessMonitor: Trend oxygenation, respiratory effort, lung sounds, blood pressure, edema, urine output, and fluid balance.
interventions: Administer ordered oxygen/diuretics and other supportive care as prescribed.
medicationSafety: Future transfusions may require individualized rate/volume strategies determined by the treating team.
teaching: Patients with heart/kidney disease should report breathing difficulty promptly during or after transfusion.
delegationScope: Recognition and escalation require licensed nursing judgment; treatment follows orders/protocol.
examTrap: Assuming every post-transfusion dyspnea is allergic or TRALI without assessing overload findings.
oneLinePearl: TACO is a transfusion plus a volume problem.

title: TRALI: Acute Lung Injury Without Simple Volume Overload
bottomLine: TRALI is a serious transfusion-related acute lung injury. New hypoxemia and respiratory distress temporally related to transfusion require immediate reaction response and urgent evaluation rather than assuming ordinary fluid overload.
recognize: Acute hypoxemia, dyspnea, bilateral pulmonary findings, and respiratory distress associated with transfusion raise concern for TRALI in the right context.
priorities: Stop the transfusion, support oxygenation/ventilation, and escalate immediately to the transfusion and clinical teams.
assessMonitor: Monitor oxygenation, respiratory effort, blood pressure, lung findings, and response to supportive care.
interventions: Prepare for higher-level respiratory support if deterioration continues.
medicationSafety: Do not automatically treat as TACO without clinical differentiation; therapies differ.
teaching: Any sudden breathing problem during or after transfusion needs urgent evaluation.
delegationScope: Reaction recognition and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Assuming crackles after transfusion always mean fluid overload.
oneLinePearl: TRALI is acute lung injury tied to transfusion, not simply too much volume.

title: Allergic Transfusion Reaction: Hives Can Escalate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Urticaria or itching may represent an allergic transfusion reaction, but wheeze, angioedema, hypotension, or respiratory compromise signals a severe reaction. Stop and escalate according to the transfusion-reaction protocol.
recognize: Pruritus, hives, flushing, angioedema, wheeze, or hypotension can occur.
priorities: Stop the transfusion and assess airway/breathing/circulation when allergic symptoms appear.
assessMonitor: Monitor skin findings, airway, respiratory status, blood pressure, and progression.
interventions: Administer ordered antihistamine/epinephrine or other emergency therapy as clinically indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not assume isolated hives will remain mild.
teaching: Tell patients to report itching or throat symptoms immediately.
delegationScope: Reaction assessment/escalation requires licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Continuing at a slower rate because the patient only has hives.
oneLinePearl: Hives may be mild; airway symptoms are not.

title: Septic Transfusion Reaction: Rigors and Shock Need Immediate Action
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: High fever, severe rigors, hypotension, nausea/vomiting, or shock during transfusion may indicate bacterial contamination/transfusion-transmitted infection. Stop the transfusion and activate the reaction/sepsis pathway immediately.
recognize: Abrupt fever and rigors with hemodynamic instability are especially concerning.
priorities: Stop transfusion, support ABCs, notify the transfusion service/provider, and follow culture/sepsis protocols.
assessMonitor: Monitor hemodynamics, temperature, mental status, perfusion, and urine output.
interventions: Prepare for ordered cultures, broad-spectrum antimicrobials, fluids, and critical-care support.
medicationSafety: Do not delay sepsis treatment while waiting for culture results when clinically indicated.
teaching: Severe chills or feeling suddenly very ill during transfusion must be reported immediately.
examTrap: Assuming fever is a benign febrile nonhemolytic reaction before instability is excluded.
oneLinePearl: Fever + rigors + hypotension during transfusion = think sepsis.

title: Febrile Nonhemolytic Reaction: Diagnose Only After Dangerous Causes Are Excluded
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fever/chills during transfusion can be febrile nonhemolytic, but hemolysis and sepsis must be considered first. Stop and evaluate according to protocol rather than assuming the benign diagnosis at bedside.
recognize: Fever and chills may occur without the severe features of hemolysis or sepsis, but overlap is substantial.
priorities: Stop the transfusion and initiate the reaction workup required by policy.
assessMonitor: Assess hemodynamics, pain, urine changes, rigors, respiratory symptoms, and progression.
interventions: Treat symptoms only after the appropriate evaluation excludes more dangerous reaction patterns.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics do not replace the transfusion-reaction evaluation.
teaching: Explain that fever during transfusion always warrants evaluation.
delegationScope: Reaction classification is not a delegated task; licensed team/provider/blood-bank evaluation is required.
examTrap: Giving acetaminophen and continuing the transfusion without evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Do not label it febrile nonhemolytic until dangerous causes are excluded.

title: Transfusion History Handoff: Prior Reactions Matter
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Prior transfusion reactions, antibodies, difficult compatibility, and special blood-product requirements must survive every transition of care. Missing history can recreate preventable risk.
recognize: Prior reaction records, antibody history, special product instructions, and blood-bank alerts are high-value handoff information.
priorities: Reconcile transfusion history before planned blood administration and communicate unresolved discrepancies.
assessMonitor: Verify prior reaction type, blood-bank notes, and current orders.
interventions: Ensure relevant history is included in handoff/discharge documentation and blood-bank communication.
medicationSafety: Do not infer that premedication or a previous uneventful transfusion eliminates current risk.
redFlags: Known antibody not reflected in current documentation
teaching: Patients should tell future clinicians about previous transfusion reactions when known.
delegationScope: History collection may be shared; verification and clinical interpretation remain licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Ignoring an old transfusion reaction because today's crossmatch is complete.
oneLinePearl: Transfusion history is a safety alert, not trivia.
